correctness.rationale: For n>=2 both statistics are means over the same unordered pairs; same-sign changes of L and E are precisely strict ranking reversals because lower L and higher E are preferred. Order one does not define these normalized metrics and poses no pairwise comparison. I inspected the proof, verification and checker and independently enumerated labeled edge sets by size, computed all-pairs distances with Floyd–Warshall, and compared integer distance sums and reciprocal sums scaled by lcm(1,...,n−1) within each (n,m). The connected counts for orders 2 through 6 were 1,4,38,728,26704; no strict reversal was found. Two distinct metric pairs split ties at six and none do earlier. At n=m=7 I reproduced the stated degree multiset and distance histograms (7,6,6,2) and (7,7,4,2,1), giving L(A)=15/7<L(B)=46/21 and E(A)=25/42<E(B)=188/315, with gaps 1/21 and 1/630. value.rationale: Matching order and edge count controls the contribution of adjacent pairs and is a natural constraint when comparing network structure. Matching degrees in the smallest witness additionally isolates arrangement from degree distribution. The precise strict boundary (as opposed to tie splitting a vertex earlier) yields a useful finite test for when the two widely used measures cannot be substituted as ranking criteria.
